Building upon recent findings by Arora et al. (2018) regarding the generalization capabilities of two-layer neural networks, this work extends those results to the setting of deep networks. Specifically, within the context of learning polynomial regression over the hypercube, the derived upper bounds on generalization error demonstrate polynomial growth with respect to the dimensionality of the domain, alongside polynomial dependence on both the depth of the network and the degree of the target polynomial. Consequently, the inherent curse of dimensionality is mitigated, suggesting that the favorable properties observed in shallow architectures persist in deeper ones. Furthermore, the dependence on the target polynomial's degree aligns with the intrinsic complexity of polynomial learning, as established in the literature.

C. elegans possesses a compact nervous system of just 302 neurons, yet it exhibits complex behaviors driven by its neural circuitry. This study aims to model these behaviors by treating the animal's brain as a black box, utilizing a deep learning framework to analyze how the system reacts to various stimuli. We constructed an artificial neural network designed to replicate the neural activity of C. elegans across a broad range of sensory inputs. Our findings indicate that Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, excel at this predictive task. By comparing these artificial models with the organism's actual biological circuitry, we observed that the RNN's structure closely mirrors the true nervous system, suggesting a high degree of similarity. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that LSTM-based neural networks serve as particularly powerful tools for understanding and simulating the response mechanisms of simple biological brains.

This research examines the combinatorial properties of a fixed point forest, a specific reduction of the permutation tree defined recursively by branching at fixed points. The study establishes that fixed forest limits exist for key metrics, including the shortest path to a leaf and the proportion of internal nodes relative to the total nodes, with all limits expressed explicitly using generating functions and prominent special functions. Furthermore, the work derives a general method for calculating the distribution of the shortest path lengths to any designated subset of nodes. The authors also provide exact counts for the total count of fixed point forests featuring a specified number of nodes and shortest leaf path length, as well as their cumulative counts. Finally, the paper concludes with several corollaries and applications derived from the main findings.

The strong Gelfand pairs of the finite special linear group $\mathrm{SL}(2,p)$ are categorized and defined, where $p$ denotes a prime number.

The classification covers both $p=2$ and odd primes. For the case of an odd prime, the classification depends on whether $p \equiv 1$ or $0 \pmod 8$. Additionally, the $\lambda$-values for the character in each strong Gelfand pair are calculated.

This paper provides fresh perspectives on the literature regarding the foundational properties of Zinbiel algebras. Specifically, it offers new proofs for the nilpotency and solvability of these algebras under the constraint of being finite-dimensional. Additionally, the authors derive fresh results concerning the modular and characteristic properties associated with the Zinbiel numbers.

This work establishes the scattering condition for the cubic inhomogeneous Schrödinger equation in the focusing regime by considering the case where $0 < p < 1/3$. By combining the well-resolved subcritical case ($p \ge 1/3$) with recent advancements in the critical case ($p < 1/3$), this study completes the characterization of scattering for all permissible values of $p$ in this setting. Specifically, it proves that in the critical scenario, scattering occurs if and only if the initial data belongs to the scattering profile manifold $ \mathcal V_{H^{s}_{x,L^{1/ ( 1 -p )} } } $ . Our methodology follows the standard profile decomposition framework, which involves analyzing the scattering behavior of the nonlinear profile and establishing uniform bounds on the scattering group for the linear profile.

We introduce DOCS, a new stochastic model of diffusion with stochastic migration that accounts for local population sizes, extending the agent-based stochastic model known as AIR. Unlike prior approaches, DOCS captures spatially dependent migration rates, allowing for a more precise analysis of local population densities. We establish exact formulas for the probability of single-type fixation, even in graphs with arbitrary topology, and provide efficient Monte Carlo algorithms for numerically computing the joint distribution of infected and susceptible fractions. Furthermore, we validate the model's performance against a wide array of network structures and migration patterns, demonstrating strong agreement with both empirical data and alternative theoretical predictions.

We introduce a novel technique for analyzing orbital resonances in multi-planet systems, utilizing Fourier series expansions of Keplerian elements to derive precise analytical expressions for planet-planet interactions. These interactions are then modeled as perturbations within a multi-body framework. We demonstrate that this approach yields results matching those of N-body simulations with the same accuracy. By applying our method, we generate resonance maps for various planetary systems, yielding insights into their formation and evolution. Specifically, we identify numerous orbital resonances in the TRAPPIST-1 system, a compact arrangement of planets orbiting an M dwarf. The resulting resonance structures in such tight orbits serve as a diagnostic tool to investigate the physical characteristics and dynamical history of exoplanetary systems.

The SLISolid Ionization Detector (SI D) functions as the principal calorimeter for the SNuBIus (SNuSI) experiment, which is a next-generation, high-luminosity facility designed to probe nucleon structure and nuclear effects within the 6–100 GeV jet energy regime. Comprising an extensive array of sampling and readout components, the system is engineered to deliver a longitudinal spatial resolution of 0.5 mm and a transverse resolution of 0.25 mm. The resulting jet energy variance is 1.0% at 100 GeV and 0.5% at 200 GeV. The paper details the design, construction, and assembly processes of the detector, along with its performance metrics derived from test-beam data. Furthermore, it outlines the strategies employed for alignment and the algorithms used for track and track-fitting to optimize data analysis.

This study employs molecular dynamics simulations to examine the phase transitions from low-density amorphous ice (LDA) and hexagonal ice (Ih) into high-density amorphous ice (HDA). The investigation utilizes a charge-transfer model to analyze the evolution of the hydrogen-bond network. The observed findings indicate that the LDA-to-HDA transformation is the converse of the Ih-to-HDA transition regarding hydrogen-bond network characteristics. Furthermore, the extent of charge transfer correlates strongly with hydrogen bond occupancy. The research also reveals that hydrogen bond occupancy serves as a reliable indicator for identifying structural transformations in both amorphous ice (LDA and HDA) and crystalline ice (Ih).

This study investigates the electronic characteristics of gold, graphite, and silicon when interfaced with a scanning tunneling microscope tip, utilizing a Scanning Tunneling Microscopy and Spectroscopy (STM/STS) approach. The analysis examines both the Local Density of States (LDOS) and electronic characteristics derived from Scanning Tunneling Spectroscopy (STS). Employing a Density Functional Theory (DFT) framework based on a model Hamiltonian, the research evaluates how the choice of substrate material influences the quantum mechanical tunneling process. The findings indicate that silicon yields the greatest LDOS, whereas gold produces the smallest. Furthermore, the work explores the relationship between the chosen material and the resulting tip reconstruction.

This study examines the reliability of informal proof annotations within the Isabelle~2005 to 2015 versions of the TPTP archive, which contains formal proofs. The authors investigate the impact of removing these informal proofs on proof verification and analyze their dependency relationships. Key findings reveal a scale-free distribution in the node in-degrees of the dependency graphs, indicating a high presence of peripheral proofs, which are characterized as those with a low likelihood of dependency. Consequently, it is concluded that the vast majority of proofs can be safely excluded from these graphs without compromising the overall consistency. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that a minimal, sufficient set of supporting proofs can be identified for any specific proof, even for those in the TPTP's core collection. The analysis also highlights the significant potential of proof automation to synthesize annotations for proofs originally provided without them.

Applying audio processing methods, specifically time scale modification, to recordings of magnetospheric ultra-low frequency (ULF) waves captured by the MMS spacecraft, creates an enhanced listening experience. This experience is designed to better illustrate the complex interactions between solar wind fluctuations and Earth's magnetic field. The techniques examined in this work are straightforward, making them easily adaptable to experimental data for educational purposes.

We employ the counterterm technique to compute the mass and angular momentum of rotating black branes carrying charge. By utilizing these quantities, we verify both the first law of black hole thermodynamics and the Smarr relation within this framework. It is important to acknowledge that the derived mass and angular momentum remain finite solely under the assumption of asymptotic flatness in the limit where the charge vanishes; consequently, the thermodynamic first law and Smarr derivation are strictly valid only for such neutral asymptotically flat configurations.

Experimental results indicate that this methodology significantly improves the effectiveness of subsequent text processing tasks. The study further examines how varying vectorization parameters and utilizing alternative Wordnet relations impact outcomes, demonstrating in conclusion that tailored adjustments can further boost the model's efficacy.

We introduce a new disk model designed to account for dust sublimation and the subsequent vertical expansion caused by radiation pressure. Utilizing a ray-tracing approach, we calculate the complex three-dimensional structure of the disk and the resulting radiative transfer. We examine the impact of the star's rotation rate and inclination angle on the disk's global morphology and spectral energy distribution. We also explore the connection between X-ray luminosity and free-free radiation components, as well as the influence of accretion luminosity on the disk's structure and spectrum.

This paper demonstrates that specific variants of Chebyshev polynomials—those of the fifth and sixth kinds—cannot be factored using the minimal polynomials associated with $\cos(\pi/m)$ values, where $m$ is an odd integer greater than one. Furthermore, we derive an identity linking these Chebyshev variants to those of the first and second kinds through the use of a rational function.

This paper introduces a novel classification framework for distinguishing between internal and non-internal faults in power generators. The method leverages stator current spectral features extracted from Finite Element Analysis (FEA) simulations. A comprehensive dataset was constructed by simulating various fault conditions and extracting their corresponding stator current spectra, which subsequently served as input for the classifier. The research evaluates multiple machine learning algorithms, including K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Decision Trees (DT), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN). Results indicate that the ANN model offers the most suitable performance for this specific task, reaching a balanced accuracy of 99.9% in identifying internal and non-internal faults. Furthermore, the study analyzes the model's behavior regarding one-sample out-of-distribution (OOD) testing scenarios.

This study presents a novel framework for mmWave multicasting systems, enabling the receiver to employ multiple antennas. Leveraging this capability, the research introduces a joint optimization framework designed to optimize both the transmit antenna selection and the resource allocation. The primary objective is to maximize the sum-rate of the system while ensuring that the transmit power budget and individual minimum rate requirements remain satisfied. To address this NP-hard challenge, the authors develop an efficient iterative algorithm. Simulation results validate the efficacy of the proposed methodology by demonstrating significant performance gains compared to baseline benchmark schemes.

We introduce a Bayesian neural network framework designed to forecast ground-state properties and identify non-trivial nuclear shell structures within the unknown region of the chart of nuclides. Trained on data from the well-charted isotopic and isospin series of alpha particles and calcium, this model extrapolates into uncharted territories extending to neutron number $N=126$ and proton number $Z=28$. Our results reveal a non-classical shell closure at $N=126$ for $^{312}\text{Pu}$ and predict the emergence of non-zero pairing gaps and non-vanishing multipole collectivities in $^{144,146}\text{Sc}$. Furthermore, we examine the reliability of these forecasts by analyzing their posterior predictive probability density distributions.

This paper introduces a new sapphire substrate, manufactured using HEMEX, which exhibits a lower loss tangent than standard EFG sapphire grown by Conticchio. The reduced loss tangent directly correlates with improved transpan qubit $T_1$ times. Additionally, we demonstrate that surface treatments applied to the HEMEX sapphire do not significantly increase loss tangent or degrade surface properties. These findings suggest that, with appropriate surface preparation, transpan qubits achieving $T_1$ relaxation times of 100 microseconds or more can be successfully fabricated on HEMEX sapphire materials.

Optical forces typically act on microscopic particles, with optical drag (pushing particles along the light path) being the standard effect. However, we report the observation of an anomalous optical drag caused by a laser beam's evanescent field, which drives a gold nanoparticle opposite to the propagation direction. This anomalous drag depends on the co-focal alignment of a counter-propagating optical counter-beam; when this counter-beam is misfocused or co-focally mismatched, the normal drag effect is restored. Conversely, when the counter-propagating field is well-focused, a conventional optical drag effect is observed. This anomalous drag effect is attributed to optical interference between the two counter-beams, which alters the local optical intensity gradient. This work introduces a novel approach for manipulating and controlling the position of microscopic particles.

This paper introduces a Lagrangian dual approach for linear robust optimization models involving binary or categorical uncertain variables, which are currently difficult to solve due to their computational inefficiency. By utilizing the Lagrangian dual, we achieve significant scalability, as the resulting model scales linearly with the number of uncertainty scenarios. We further propose a subgradient-based decomposition algorithm that separates the solution process into two components: an aggregate master problem and individual subproblems, each corresponding to one uncertainty. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this method substantially outperforms existing state-of-the-art solvable approaches for standard cases.

This paper introduces a Social Sentiment Analysis (SSA) framework designed to analyze public opinion trends through social media activity. The primary objective is to examine sentiment fluctuations by leveraging relevant hashtags and keywords. The proposed methodology comprises three core phases: (1) identifying pertinent hashtags via information gain analysis, (2) performing sentiment classification on relevant tweets using a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model, and (3) visualizing the aggregated sentiment trends via a heatmap. Validating this approach, we tested it against Twitter data collected during the 2019 George Floyd protests, demonstrating the framework's efficacy in operational environments.

Unsupervised learning techniques are widely recognized for their capacity to identify structured information within complex datasets. This study introduces a novel perspective on these methods, conceptualizing them as processes that traverse the space of possible patterns, guided by the specific characteristics of the input data. This framework serves as a unifying approach for various machine learning applications, spanning from clustering and dimensionality reduction to automatic feature extraction. Furthermore, it enables a more profound understanding of both algorithmic behavior and the broader field of data mining.

This study investigates the transferability of Graph Neural Network (GNN) knowledge across community-structured graphs via multiple transfer learning benchmarks. Our findings indicate that the potential for transferring insights from a source to a target task is dictated by community structure similarity, which can be assessed using proposed metrics. Furthermore, by integrating community structure information into a graph alignment strategy, we achieved an enhanced transfer learning performance.

We introduce an Indian feature process (IFFP) that extends the Indian buffet process (MacKay and Neal, 2004) by associating users and items with latent feature groups rather than individual binary indicators. In this framework, each group functions as a latent cluster of features, and the probability of a specific feature within the cluster varies per user and per item. Unlike standard IBP, the IFFP explicitly models sparse interactions between users and items, making it particularly suitable for high-dimensional domains like recommender systems where data is sparse. We further develop a Bayesian nonparametric model that integrates the IFFP with a collaborative filtering framework, featuring a new latent low-rank matrix that acts as an item-user kernel. This kernel utilizes group-level sparsity to enhance predictions. The proposed approach is evaluated on multiple recommendation benchmarks, demonstrating that it outperforms standard baselines, especially in scenarios characterized by extreme sparsity.

The mostly set disjointness problem functions similarly to the traditional set disjointness problem, which involves two parties, Alice and Bob, receiving inputs $x$ and $y$ that represent subsets of a universe $U$ (typically binary strings of length $n$). The goal is to determine if the union of their input sets contains any element shared by both, i.e., if $| (x \cup y) \cap y | > 0$. However, in the mostly set disjointness variant, the inputs are guaranteed to contain exactly one unique element, meaning exactly one index $i$ satisfies the condition that the $i$-th bit of both $x$ and $y$ equals 1. This problem has been extensively analyzed in communication complexity, a field examining the difficulty of solving computational tasks where multiple parties exchange information. This paper introduces a novel algorithmic framework for addressing mostly set disjointness that utilizes a specific type of nonnegative kernel function. This kernel function, which resembles the classic "inner product" but is distinct in its application, is designed to identify the unique element $i$ that is shared by the two input sets. This approach is significant because it is the first instance of a classical algorithm solving mostly set disjointness that is not restricted to quantum computing paradigms. This work is further relevant to quantum communication complexity, a field investigating algorithmic challenges in quantum information exchange scenarios.

This work examines the paramagnetic phase of a spin-1 ferromagnetic system subjected to the influence of both thermal fluctuations and weak magnetic fields. By utilizing the generalized mean-field theory, the study derives the critical exponents $\nu$, $z$, and $\theta$. Specifically, the analysis reveals the relationship $\nu + \theta = 1$ and calculates the dynamical critical exponent $y_t = 2$. Furthermore, the research investigates the effects of a position-dependent mass on these critical properties, demonstrating that the critical exponents themselves remain unchanged despite the spatial variation in mass.

This work presents a proposed apparatus for generating macroscopic quantum entanglement between traveling matter waves of single neutral atoms and their stationary counterparts trapped in a chip-based optical potential. The setup achieves coupling between the motional modes of two atoms, each residing in a distinct quantum state within the same trap. By utilizing a standing wave pulsed beam (VBS) to interact with both atoms, the system creates nonclassical correlations between their individual motions. These correlated motions then serve as quantum inputs for a beam splitter, resulting in entanglement between the free-moving atoms and the atoms remaining confined in the trap. Ultimately, the article outlines a strategy for producing and characterizing these persistent, trap-based atom-field entangled states.

The many-electron anomalous velocity plays a pivotal role in the understanding of diverse physical phenomena, ranging from the Hall effect across single-band systems to unified models encompassing multi-band and two-dimensional materials with spin-orbit coupling, as well as the anomalous contribution to the inverse spin Hall effect. This study demonstrates that the anomalous velocity's role in the Hall effect is universal across all three system types. Furthermore, it elucidates specific manifestations of the anomalous contribution to the inverse spin Hall effect within two of these frameworks.

In the treatment of respiratory failure, mechanical ventilation is a critical therapy that delivers air to the lungs using a device that synchronizes with the patient's natural breathing rhythm. This device regulates the volume of air per breath (tidal volume) and the rate of ventilation. This paper introduces a strategy to utilize two-way valves to enable a single ventilator to support multiple patients simultaneously, each receiving tailored tidal volumes. The system ensures synchronized breaths and prevents tidal mixing between the ventilator and the patient. The proposed method is validated using simulations for two scenarios: ventilation for three individuals and a hybrid setup involving one ventilator and two patients. The results confirm the efficacy of this single-ventilator, two-valve system in managing simultaneous ventilation for multiple individuals under varied operational modes.

For a generic two-parameter family of real cubic rational maps, we demonstrate that every iterate possesses deck transformation groups that form nested congrence subgroups within the modular group. We also address the problem of determining monodromy groups for higher-degree cubic rational maps, particularly those that are bicritical. For real rational maps of degree $d \ge 2$ possessing two critical values, the action of the monodromy group on the map's fibers generates a covering of the twice-punctured complex plane. We prove that for sequences of real bicritical maps where the degree $d$ tends to infinity, these coverings converge to levels of the congruence subgroups within various congrential families of the modular group.

This study examines the electronic and optical properties of tungsten-based transition metal dichalcogenides (MoS$_2$, MoSe$_2$, WS$_2$, WSe$_2$) using first-principles density functional theory. We demonstrate that these materials' work functions, ionization energies, and electron affinities are thickness-dependent, scaling inversely with chalcogen layer count. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that excitonic and triton resonances significantly influence the optical absorption spectra of these systems.

As a general approach, delta lenses can be parameterized with an asymmetry, allowing the various components of the asymmetric delta lens pattern to be unified under the concept of an "asymmetric delta lens monad." Additionally, we demonstrate that asymmetric delta lenses can be effectively represented using co-simplicial structures, enabling the application of existing literature involving symmetric delta lenses to this context.

The accuracy of estimating oscillatory integrals via the method of stationary phase is governed by the degree of smoothness required for the phase and amplitude functions. We present refined estimates that lower these regularity constraints by employing techniques such as Fourier transform analysis in addition to Fourier series. Furthermore, we apply these improvements to two specific cases: one-dimensional integrals oscillating along a closed curve and a framework for oscillatory integrals defined over manifolds.

This study introduces a generalized synthetic iteration scheme (GSIS) designed to accelerate convergence and enhance efficiency in simulating rarefied gas dynamics. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on multiple iterations to achieve convergence, the proposed GSIS employs the small perturbation theory to update flow properties within the shock layer based on shock parameters, streamlining the process into a single iteration. The framework is versatile, capable of modeling oblique and normal shocks across one and two dimensions. A key advantage of the GSIS is its ability to precisely capture shock structures with minimal grid resolution, significantly reducing the number of required computational nodes. The method's accuracy and computational efficiency were validated through simulations of normal and oblique shocks, which were benchmarked against experimental data.

To address why the cosmological amounts of dark matter and visible matter remain similar, the axion quark nuggets (AQNs) model proposes that dark matter consists of compact, macroscopic objects formed from visible baryons. While this solution eliminates the need for entirely new physics to account for dark matter, it significantly elevates the importance of the QCD vacuum structure. This paper reviews key aspects of the AQN framework, including the nESM model, and outlines several open questions regarding the phenomenon.

CMS analysis of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, totaling 35.9 inverse femtobarns of data, reveals a resonance in the Higgs-like boson mass region. This state, decaying into photon pairs, is observed at 750 GeV with a statistical significance of 4.1 sigma. Distinguishing this from the standard model Higgs, the new particle shows a branching ratio for photon decay 40 to 50 times greater. Analysis of production modes indicates a cross-section 10 to 100 times greater than that predicted for photon fusion of a standard model state. These findings suggest the resonance may be a composite or Kaluza-Klein state arising from extra dimensions or other beyond-standard-model dynamics.

This constraint ensures their equivalence regarding both homotopy groups and quasitopological homotopy groups. We also provide a concrete example of a sequence of fibrations that remains invariant across both standard homotopy groups and quasitopological homotopy groups, yet exhibit rigidity only in the quasi-topological context.

"In an experiment, we engineered Pauli crystals of ultra-cold fermions by pairing a two-dimensional square-lattice of optical potential with a spin-1/2 atoms possessing three degenerate states. By utilizing Pauli blocking effects, we isolated one specific spin component within a separate plane parallel to the optical structure, resulting in the formation of these crystalline structures. We demonstrate that the remaining two spin components behave as adjustable parameters that dictate the macroscopic properties of the system. By manipulating these degrees of freedom, we can transition the assembly from a three-dimensional spin-wave fluid into an exotic quantum state characterized by coupled spin and charge density waves."

This paper introduces a new predictive algorithm based on the discrete fourth-order explicit Runge-Kutta method, designed to address the symbolic matrix exponential model of the index-1 state-dependent linear differential equation (ODE) framework. This approach is applied to construct a predictive Zettell-type neural algorithm (ZNN) capable of forecasting the predictive state of the index-1 ODE system. Unlike traditional ODE integration methods that rely on iterative techniques, this model enables the prediction of future states at arbitrary future times, $t_{k+1}$, using the current state at $t_k$. Furthermore, a novel error estimation scheme is developed to determine the optimal update interval, $\Delta t$, ensuring the total approximation error remains below a predetermined tolerance threshold. Numerical simulations are conducted to validate the method's effectiveness and performance.

Wolter I mirrors, which function as X-ray telescopes, are mathematically defined by conic sections. However, when modeling these optics in ray tracing software, the conic sections are frequently approximated using higher-order polynomials to enhance fitting precision. This study examines the relationship between such polynomials and Wolter I geometries to determine the most effective polynomial representation for designing telescope mirrors. The findings indicate that while hyperbolic mirrors (used in focal length configurations) can be accurately replicated by adding polynomial terms to a hyperbola, elliptical mirrors (used in off-axis configurations) are best modeled by superimposing two closely placed conic sections rather than through high-order polynomial expansion.

Moiré systems are renowned for generating strongly correlated phases, exemplified by moiré magnets, which feature reentrant ground states that return at higher Coulomb interaction strengths after melting out intermediate phases. This study investigates a one-dimensional moiré structure composed of two layers of Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chains, identifying a similar reentrant ground state under Coulomb coupling. We employ a variational approach utilizing generalized mean-field theory combined with BCS mean-field formalism to explore these phenomena. Furthermore, we examine how varying optical phonon interactions influences the system, revealing a distinct phonon-induced reentrant ground state.

This paper introduces a steganographic system designed for concealing and communicating encrypted messages within grayscale images. It employs an enhanced version of the adaptive least significant bit (ALSB) algorithm to increase capacity, combined with selective DCT coefficients to boost robustness. To further improve robustness, the system applies the concept of error correction from the Hamming code. This approach achieves a message capacity 2.33 times greater than that of the original ALSB method while maintaining similar levels of robustness. For messages with Hamming code-compatible lengths, successful decoding is achieved with an error correction capability of up to 12.67%.

This paper introduces a machine learning approach to unit commitment that specifically targets operational constraint screening. By leveraging the inherent structure of these problems, we train models to predict whether specific constraints will be violated for a given subset of variables. We evaluate two learning paradigms: an unsupervised method that generates feature spaces for direct application to MILP solvers, and a supervised approach designed to create data-driven screening precursors. Numerical results across various test systems demonstrate that this approach effectively reduces computational times by minimizing the number of iterations required to solve the commitment problem.

The $\eta$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ single crystal was synthesized via a high-pressure and high-temperature method, with its structure confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. Its physical properties were investigated using various experimental techniques, including powder neutron diffraction, specific heat, magnetization, and electrical resistance measurements. At ambient pressure, $\eta$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ undergoes a second-order phase transition below 0.4 K to a monoclinic structure (space group $P2_1$, Z = 4), accompanied by a slight monoclinic distortion. Upon applying hydrostatic pressure exceeding 1.2 GPa, the material transforms into an orthorhombic phase (space group $Cmcm$, Z = 4) through a first-order transition. This transformation is accompanied by a significant surge in electrical resistance and a sharp drop in the specific heat capacity. The study further explores the interplay between pressure and quantum fluctuations in driving this phase transition.

Synthetic control methods rely on weighting a donor pool of control units to create a counterfactual that approximates the target unit. While prior Synthetic Control implementations have been constrained to usable units due to the risk of negative or probabilities exceeding one, this approach is suboptimal given that excluded units possess valuable pre-intervention information. To address this, we present a Synthetic Estimator using Weighted Donors and a Counterfactual Anchor (SEWDA), which leverages Linear Programming to incorporate previously unusable units in the weight estimation process. Donor selection occurs in two phases: first, SEWDA applies optimization to determine weights for the previously unusable units by applying a penalty to the inclusion of the previously usable units; second, these weights serve as a fixed anchor in a subsequent optimization that calculates final weights for the previously usable units. SEWDA offers a practical, no-parameter alternative to prior Synthetic Estimator approaches, effectively utilizing the entire donor pool to generate more precise counterfactuals.

This study addresses the challenge of learning from graph-structured data while ensuring local differential privacy (LDP) for sensitive nodes. We introduce an LDP-enabled algorithm for semi-supervised graph classification designed to preserve privacy without compromising classification accuracy. Additionally, we provide theoretical performance bounds and validate our approach through experiments on various real-world datasets.

This study examines how the Carrier Envelope Phase (CPEP) influences ionization and tunneling electron dynamics within plasma bubbles generated by high-intensity, short-pulse lasers operating in a vacuum. It is established that CEP variations significantly alter the shape of these bubbles and induce variations in secondary electron emission. Regarding ionization, there is a consistent trend showing that ion clouds form more compactly as the pulse propagates when CEP increases. Conversely, higher CEP values shift the primary mode of bubble formation from ionization to tunneling electron dynamics. It is further demonstrated that CEP changes can suppress the formation of secondary electron clouds surrounding the primary ion clouds. In a vacuum, CEP acts as a critical parameter in shaping plasma bubble structures and regulating the transition between distinct electron dynamics mechanisms.

This study outlines the principles for creating a specialized $2\mu$ and $0\mu$ electron capture (EC) $\beta^-$-decay detector. We analyze the detection capabilities for $2\mu$ and $0\mu$ EC states, demonstrating that $0\mu$ sensitivity is significantly more sensitive to EC occurring in outer electron shells. Consequently, we argue that the detector's $0\mu$ sensitivity can be substantially improved by utilizing EC sources characterized by valence electron configurations.

This paper introduces a novel approach to image colorization that surpasses prior methods by employing a more versatile framework. At its core, the approach utilizes a deep neural network to predict an energy function governing the relationship between colorization fidelity and specific constraints like the input grayscale image or semantic color labels. This energy function is subsequently minimized to generate the final colored output. A key advantage of the method lies in its ability to accept arbitrary auxiliary constraints—such as depth maps, normal maps, or instance segmentation maps—in addition to standard inputs, thereby enhancing colorization fidelity. Furthermore, the framework supports an end-to-end trainable architecture capable of jointly optimizing the neural network and the energy function. Experiments on the challenging Colorization at Height (CAH) benchmark demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, with additional qualitative results confirming superior visual quality on diverse datasets including City.gr and challenging historical imagery.

The n-dimensional Hamiltonian Ermakov system exhibits dynamic equivalence to a specific configuration of the generalized space as a background, with transformations acting on this space inducing the system's equations of motion. Consequently, we can analyze the dynamics of the n-dimensional Hamiltonian Ermakov system by studying the equivalent geometric setting. This equivalence allows for the derivation of first integrals, first-order systems, and complete sets of independent, Hamiltonian-conserving integrals for the system. Based on the count of these classification integrals, we categorize the n-dimensional Hamiltonian Ermakov system into three types: integrable, partially integrable, and non-integrable. Furthermore, the study identifies a particular three-dimensional Hamiltonian Ermakov system that exhibits integrability.

The escalating demand for public transport information stems from growing user expectations, yet traditional methods often fail to address this need effectively. Consequently, new approaches utilizing data mining and machine learning have emerged to enhance both service delivery and information accessibility. This paper introduces a practical application of one such method: a mobile web service designed to analyze user queries and deliver tailored public transit updates. By leveraging data mining and machine learning algorithms, the system identifies patterns in passenger queries to optimize the generation of transit information. The study details the architecture, implementation, and operational results of a real-world prototype developed in a medium-sized city in the Republic of Ireland. The authors conclude that these innovative methodologies significantly improve the capacity to meet the public's information requirements within public transportation ecosystems.

Recent efforts in few-shot learning have concentrated on refining classification strategies to better leverage support samples. However, these methods often overlook a critical challenge: the presence of outlier samples within the few support set, which can degrade performance. To address this, we introduce a novel framework that integrates both query and support augmentation to filter out anomalies. Specifically, a quantile-based approach is employed to identify outlying data points, while a generator-based architecture is utilized to synthesize queries and supports that remain close to the actual data distribution. By generating such representative samples, the technique effectively mitigates the adverse impact caused by identified outliers. Extensive experiments on standard few-shot benchmarks demonstrate that our method attains state-of-the-art performance.

We investigate how the non-invertible charge defects identified in [arXiv:2109.08968] behave when placed in contact with a local current operator. Demonstrating that the current operator alters the defect's fusion rules and braiding characteristics, we show that proximity to a current operator effectively restores broken symmetries and establishes the corresponding order parameter. Finally, we examine the implications of these findings for charge order and symmetry breaking within lattice models.

The concept of semi-transitive graphs emerged in the 1980s from the study of odd cycles mod 2, a structure that defines split graphs as the union of a clique and an independent set. While split graphs are trivially semi-transitive, the central inquiry is determining how large an independent set a general semi-transitive graph can possess. This paper addresses three main areas: first, it establishes that semi-transitive split-graph orientation is achievable and provides a linear-time algorithm for verifying this property in split graphs; second, it proves that among graphs with a maximum independent set of size $k$, only finitely many distinct types exist, allowing for recognition in $O(n^2)$ time. Consequently, graphs with a small independent set ($k$) are characterized by a specific class of split subgraphs and a bounded collection of non-split subgraphs, each of size $O(k^2)$. Finally, the study derives structural properties for split-free semi-split graphs, which are defined by a bounded diameter and limited path lengths.

The analysis focused on decays of $Z$ bosons into tau-lepton pairs ($ZZ$) and involved jets from $Z$ bosons ($Z$) to distinguish between genuine and fake taus. This study introduces a method for applying Bayesian Neural Networks to astrophysical data, leveraging their classification probability distributions to calculate classifier uncertainty. This measured uncertainty facilitates active learning by guiding the selection of new data points that most effectively refine the Bayesian classification model. As an application, we address the challenge of identifying transient events in the Gaia Data Release 2, utilizing the method to improve the precision of the active learning process and subsequently enhancing the overall classification accuracy of the neural network.

Intermodal Brillouin scattering, driven by counter-propagating light modes with differing spatial distributions, is a critical phenomenon in photonic structures. In this study, we reveal that asymmetric mechanical modes, such as anti-symmetric flexural shapes, can suppress interactions between symmetric optical modes by nullifying their overlap integral. This insight is validated through experiments on suspended silicon nitride membranes, where a specific anti-symmetric mechanical mode effectively suppresses intermodal Brillouin scattering between co-propagating symmetric optical modes. The observed results align perfectly with theoretical predictions, offering a novel strategy for the tailored control of optical-mechanical coupling in devices.

This study introduces a local search algorithm, referred to as E2LS, which integrates the strengths of both complete and incomplete search strategies to address the Signed Universe Knapsack (SUKP) and Balanced Maximum Cut (BMCP) challenges. The primary objective of E2LS is to identify a high-quality feasible solution quickly and, if feasible within a set timeframe, converge toward an optimal solution. The technique operates by executing unrestricted neighborhood searches initially to locate a solution of high quality, followed by restricted neighborhood searches that maintain feasibility under time constraints. Experimental evaluations against the state-of-the-art algorithm, LSH, reveal that E2LS achieves superior performance in solving both SUKP and BMCP instances.

This study introduces Chis, a new churn prevention model that leverages time-series data. Our findings indicate that utilizing training history for time-series events enhances both the accuracy of predictions and the model's ability to identify at-risk churners. We examine how varying the length of training history impacts results and assess the influence of different time-series preprocessing techniques on model performance. Additionally, we implement a dynamic training history approach, utilizing variable-length input based on the most recent activity of each customer. This adaptive strategy further boosts performance compared to static fixed-length methods.

We examine the perturbative renormalization group (RG) flow of the Effective Field Theory (EFT) within the Ising Fixed Point (IFP) framework, specifically analyzing the impact of an irrelevant perturbation $L_{-4}\bar{L}_{-4}\Theta$. Our results indicate that this term does not restore the IFP's integrability, thereby precluding an exact solution for the flow equations. Consequently, EFT remains the most viable option for numerically simulating the IFP when dealing with operators possessing non-local spatial structures.

This paper presents a factorization formula linking gluon TMD gluon PDFs across the Kinematic schemes light-cone gauge and Coulomb gauge. In addition, the text provides the corresponding light-cone gauge relation to collinear gluon PDFs. These relationships facilitate the computation of gluin TMD gluins using lattice gluon field configurations within either gauge, thereby enabling the derivation of nonperturb gluon TM gluins.

We have developed a novel Monte Carlo simulation to examine how electrons and positrons from muon pairs are affected by the electromagnetic fields of nearby nuclei, a process essential for interpreting electron-positron spectra in light nuclei collisions. While the electromagnetic fields of the target nucleus are typically accounted for using Fermi functions, those generated by the projectile nucleus are often neglected. We demonstrate that incorporating these previously ignored fields significantly reshapes the transverse momentum profiles of electrons and positrons within the spectrum. Additionally, our analysis reveals systematic discrepancies between experimental measurements and theoretical model predictions for electron-positron spectra in ${}^{12}\text{C}+{}^{12}\text{C}$ collisions at 100 A MeV when the projectile-induced Fermi function is excluded. We find that including these interactions aligns the model calculations closely with the observed spectral data.

Cycling is a highly effective, eco-friendly mode of travel that is gaining popularity in cities. However, current infrastructure and safety standards often fail to meet demand, necessitating the collection of extensive data to inform urban planning and improve cycling conditions. This study introduces the "Cycling Urban Planning for Efficiency and Safety" (CUPES) framework, which leverages data collected from cyclists equipped with smartphones to enhance infrastructure, boost safety, and support data-driven urban planning. By utilizing off-the-shelf device sensors, the approach gathers information on cyclist behavior, road surface conditions, and environmental factors to inform maintenance schedules and emergency responses. The research also analyzes correlations between cycling speed, road conditions, and environmental variables to develop a speed-based regression model. Validated using real-world datasets, this model successfully predicts speed variations caused by infrastructure issues and adverse weather, with results demonstrating that the model's accuracy surpasses that of existing benchmarks.

This paper introduces a robust, data-driven safe and optimal path planning framework designed for complex robotic systems with unknown models. By leveraging extensive historical operational data to identify system characteristics, the study addresses model uncertainties that impact robotic performance. These uncertainties are integrated into a robust control architecture, where the robust terminal invariant set (RTIS) serves as the robust control barrier function (RCBF) to ensure path safety. Furthermore, a data-driven algorithm is utilized to calculate the maximal RTIS, thereby optimizing the control inputs. Theoretical proofs confirm that the synthesized control strategy guarantees both robustness against model inaccuracies and safety for the trajectories. Simulation experiments validate the efficacy of the proposed methodology.

This paper introduces the concept of "adversarily robust representations," where the training objective limits the model's ability to create adversarial examples by the network itself. We demonstrate that neural networks employing identity mappings inherently satisfy the necessary conditions for achieving such representation-based constraints on adversarial failure. Consequently, models with identity mappings are unable to define their own robust boundaries in an adversarial manner. While these models remain theoretically susceptible to adversarial attacks of any magnitude, we show empirically that adding random noise during the training phase significantly diminishes their vulnerability. This finding suggests that although identity mappings limit self-generated adversarial examples, noisy training serves as an effective strategy to further strengthen the overall adversarial robustness of such models.

This note establishes that for every such surface, DIR points constitute a set with full measure among its (countably many) homotopy classes of loxodromic isometries. Multivariate data analysis often necessitates a data-driven approach to uncover hidden structures and relationships. This study introduces a novel method for constructing connectivity networks using Total Correlation (TC) as a metric for multivariate dependence. By integrating information across all variables, TC offers a comprehensive view of connectivity, addressing limitations found in pairwise measures like Pearson correlation which overlook multivariate interactions. Consequently, TC-based networks can reveal connectivity patterns associated with brain changes and pathologies, serving as biomarkers for clinical applications in areas such as neuroimaging and clinical trials. The paper demonstrates the efficacy of this TC-based methodology through a case study on Alzheimer's disease, analyzing functional connectivity in the resting states of both healthy individuals and patients.

We demonstrate that Clifford algebra-valued functions which are square-integrable across $n=1,2,3$ dimensions with respect to the standard Euclidean metric form complete orthogonal sets relative to the associated inner product space. In these specific dimensions, every square-integrable function can be expressed as an infinite series converging to terms defined by these functions. Furthermore, in addition to these conditions, these functions satisfy the associated partial differential equations.

Sampling from Gaussian processes (GPs) incurs high computational costs, particularly when dealing with large datasets. Pathwise conditioning addresses this by enabling the efficient generation of posteroi samples through the construction of a set of correlated paths. This technique is especially advantageous for tasks like computer emulations and Bayesian optimization, where the conditioning paths are fixed and invariant. However, existing implementations often fail to leverage these pre-known trajectories fully, resulting in redundant, unnecessary forward passes. This inefficiency becomes critical when the path length is substantial. This paper introduces a new method: "pathwise conditioning with adaptive forward passes." By estimating the variance of GP predictions along a condition path and using this metric to determine sampling needs, the technique only executes forward passes in regions of high uncertainty. Leveraging the Gaussian process property that predictive variance decreases as more observations are collected, the approach adaptively reduces computational load in areas already well-explored. Consequently, this adaptive strategy significantly accelerates sampling compared to current methods, which neglect the efficiency potential of known paths.

This paper introduces a two-ray (TR) model designed to forecast received signal power (RSP) for communication links between UAVs and ground sensors. It introduces a specific UAV coverage metric grounded in the calculated RSP, accounting for both sensor placement and the flight path of the aerial platform. A primary objective is to minimize the total RSP variance across all sensors, thereby enhancing communication stability. To achieve this, we formulate a trajectory optimization problem that incorporates RSP variance minimization alongside practical flight constraints. Furthermore, we develop an efficient iterative algorithm to determine an optimal flight path, accompanied by theoretical proof confirming its convergence. Simulation outcomes validate that the proposed framework effectively boosts communication robustness while maintaining fuel efficiency.

The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is engineered to operate as a premier neutrino factory, capable of probing physics far beyond the Standard Model, including searching for rare events like proton decay. Its massive 4,400-ton liquid argon time-projection chamber (LArTPC) offers exceptional sensitivity to these ultra-sparse signals. The detector's ability to distinguish between nitrogen and argon within the dense liquid allows the system to precisely identify proton decay signatures. The LArTPC's granular spatial resolution and sensitivity to specific decay modes enable the detection of the resulting final states with high efficiency. The analysis focuses on the observable final states produced by the primary proton decay channels: $p \to \pi^0 e^+$ and $p \to \bar{\nu} \nu e^+$. The study evaluates the detector's performance by examining its response to both the signal and the dominant background sources. The results demonstrate that DUNE is exceptionally well-suited to identify these decay events, with the detector's response being well-modeled and the signal-to-background ratio remaining favorable.

This study introduces a novel approach to SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), a leading machine learning framework for feature importance, by incorporating a time dimension. By extending SHAP with temporal aspects, we enable not only a measurement of feature relevance but also an analysis of its evolution over time. This specific extension, named TimeSHAP, integrates seamlessly into existing explainable AI (XAI) visualization tools. We demonstrate this capability by applying TimeSHAP to two distinct datasets: a real-world credit risk dataset and a synthetic electrocardiogram (ECG) dataset. The analysis reveals how features gain relevance over time and highlights critical shifts in that relevance, thereby validating the method's potential for dynamic model interpretation.

The V&O (Variation & Instantiation) framework addresses the need for managing diverse abstractions and instantiations within object-oriented systems. In the VO (Variation Viewpoint) approach, object orientation is extended to explicitly model variation. VO development is viewed as the progressive refinement of variation views, which represent different perspectives on a variation model regarding specific concerns. These views are partially ordered based on refinement, and the process involves abstracting away variation details to simplify complexity for certain aspects while retaining it for others. Consequently, the framework supports various design patterns, such as abstracting variation via interfaces or encapsulating variation in specific classes. This paper introduces a new set of view-to-view and model-to-model transformations designed to facilitate the conversion between different abstraction levels. These transformations are defined using the VO notation and formalized within a formal framework. The approach is demonstrated through an application analyzing the evolution of the VO framework's internal views, alongside a reference framework built in Python.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success across numerous domains, yet its sample complexity remains a significant challenge. This issue is particularly acute in complex environments, such as those encountered in Atari games, where acquiring data is costly. Although recent research has proposed various strategies to enhance sample efficiency, they often struggle with high variance in policy gradient estimations. This paper introduces VRER, a novel framework designed to mitigate this variance while maintaining the agent's exploration capabilities through experience replay. By employing a loss function that incorporates the variance of the gradient estimator, we derive an optimal update rule that reduces variance without compromising sample utilization. Additionally, we propose a practical method for approximating the expected variance and provide a theoretical convergence analysis along with empirical validation using the Stable-Baselines3 library on both Mujoco and Atari tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that VRER achieves superior sample efficiency compared to existing methods.

We provide a straightforward and rigorous proof in one dimension that establishes the equivalence between a generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula derived in one dimension for one-dimensional fermionic systems. This derivation is built upon the observation that both the finite-dimensional integral and the original fermionic path integral can be linked to conformal field theories in one-dimensional space. This approach yields natural extensions of bosonization to advanced contexts such as finite temperature scenarios and systems exhibiting fermionization.

This paper introduces a novel deep spatiotemporal learning framework designed to predict the future frames of a video sequence. Central to our approach is the Detail Context Block (DCB), a specific set of selected spatio-temporal features extracted from a network processing adjacent time steps. By feeding these selected features alongside current image data into a predictor, the model effectively leverages crucial fine-grained details that standard Context Blocks often overlook due to their reliance on entire volumes of data. Extensive experiments conducted on the DeepFaceDeviding (DFD) benchmark demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches, yielding improvements of 1.5% to 2.5% in Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR).

In languages like C, where memory is explicitly managed, type systems can effectively ensure both data and memory safety. However, in function-first languages such as Haskell, where functions are primary, data structures often undergo explicit memory management, making it difficult to apply types to operations that involve this management. Consequently, existing research has largely focused on functional languages that rely solely on immutable data. In contrast, this paper introduces a static type system designed for an explicit, functional version of the "let-binding" construct. By formalizing this bind construct within a call-by-name lambda calculus, we enable the flow of mutable state while preserving the language's safety guarantees. Our approach utilizes "affine" typing to restrict the lifespan of mutable state to a single execution thread. We further augment this system with an explicit effect framework to provide finer-grained control over when side effects occur.

We demonstrate that lepton number violation can be implemented at the lowest level through the addition of exactly two heavy neutral leptons, which possess Majorana masses. This construction maintains the inclusion of all existing Standard Model interactions alongside the newly introduced heavy neutral leptons. The analysis indicates that, in the presence of these neutral leptons, the resulting Higgs potential exhibits a first-order electroweak phase transition. Furthermore, the study establishes the necessary criteria for this phase transition to proceed adiabatically and satisfy the requirements for successful baryogenesis.

This study suggests a novel, near-linear-time algorithm for decoding pre-transformed polar codes, such as CRC-aided polar codes, leveraging the successive cancellation list (SCL) framework. The proposed method demonstrates significant performance gains, offering roughly a 0.3 dB improvement in bit-error-rate (BER) at 0.001 error probability compared to previous approaches. The algorithm's efficiency stems from the strategic pre-computation of specific values during the SCL process. Furthermore, we present a further enhancement to this scheme and validate its performance through simulations on a 5G NR LDPC code system.

We have conducted a study to evaluate the performance of various nonlinear coaddition techniques—specifically median, clipped-mean, and weighted sigma-clipped mean—across 1000 synthetic galaxies and stars generated using realistic simulations. The analysis reveals that while these algorithms successfully suppress stellar variability in coadds, they introduce a systematic bias by failing to preserve a consistent Point Spread Function (PSF) profile across the coadd image. This mismatch causes the effective point spread function (ePSF) to fluctuate depending on the specific coadd position, thereby degrading the precision of photometric measurements. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a novel method that calculates the effective PSF based on the individual image PSFs of all contributing exposures within each coadd. When applied, this approach yields consistent photometric precision across different locations in the coadd image.

Fracture initiates at a notch tip due to sharpening instability, a phenomenon where a material's tendency to form sharper notches under specific loads drives further sharpness. This study investigates the sharpening instability of notches within elastic-brittle materials, specifically those exhibiting a size-dependent strength criterion. By applying a criterion based on a critical external energy release rate, we demonstrate that such notches experience sharpening instability regardless of whether the material is homogeneous or graded. Furthermore, a necessary condition for this instability is derived, and a specific formula for the critical external release rate is established. Additionally, the work analyzes how this instability influences the fracture strength of notched slabs, providing a theoretical framework to explain the observed phenomenon.

We introduce an approach to chrodeal surface Schramm–Loewner evolutions (sLEs) by utilizing boundary imaginary surfaces, a concept originally developed by Kozma and V\'{e}'er\'{e}'s. This study establishes the almost sure uniqueness of sLEs derived from imaginary surfaces involving Brownian motions on the imaginary plane, while also demonstrating their fractal nature and a self-similarity property.

This paper examines the large-time behavior of the Navier-Stokes equations with initial data in $L^q$ spaces ($1 \le q < 3$) that remain bounded away from equilibrium. It is demonstrated that, for sufficiently large times, the solution's maximum norm of derivatives exhibits linear growth relative to the initial data's maximum norm. Specifically, a precise asymptotic expansion is derived for such solutions.

This paper introduces a new Classical-Variable Quantum Computing (CVQC) circuit-based verification protocol. It is designed to efficiently and accurately assess the fidelity of linear optical operations. The method leverages the inherent properties of Gaussian states and the classical-interpretation of these distributions to create a procedure that is both rapid and precise. Specifically, the protocol achieves linear time complexity, $O(N)$, for the processing of $N$ optical modes, making it highly scalable. The implementation was validated using a photonic setup executing a 4-mode single-mode Squeezed State. Results demonstrate that the single-shot frame potential estimation attained an accuracy of 98.7%, while Monte Carlo simulations achieved 99.99% accuracy. The estimated gate performance reached approximately 99.9999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999999

This paper introduces LC4IoT, a blockchain consensus protocol tailored for supply chain applications that enhances performance by leveraging the specific attributes of Internet of Things (IoT) nodes. The protocol's primary innovation is a novel validation mechanism that utilizes a distributed clock system to synchronize block assembly timing, effectively reducing computational latency and overhead. Additionally, LC4 incorporates an optimized transaction ordering strategy designed to further minimize delay and resource consumption. Comparative analyses against established consensus algorithms demonstrate that LC4 significantly surpasses them in terms of speed and efficiency while preserving robust security and immutability.

Cell tracking and segmentation are fundamental to image analysis in biomedical research. Although deep generative models have recently emerged as a promising approach for synthesizing realistic cellular structures, their application to biological contexts remains under-explored. This study introduces a neural network-based deep generative model capable of producing plausible cell shapes, which is trained on real cellular imagery. The synthesized shapes are then integrated into existing cell tracking and segmentation frameworks to evaluate their efficacy. Our results indicate that adding synthetic cell shapes enhances the accuracy of both cell tracking and segmentation. This improvement stems from the fact that synthetic shapes bridge gaps caused by missing cells in images, thereby reducing uncertainty in predicting cell trajectories and refining the precision of segmentation for neighboring cells.

Scientific literature is vital to scientific and technological advancement, yet individuals with visual impairments often face significant difficulties navigating its internal references (such as citations and cross-sections) due to navigation obstacles in digital formats. We propose employing computer vision techniques to enable a mobile device's camera to automatically identify and locate these internal visual references within document text, allowing the user to view them directly on a connected screen. We have developed a system capable of identifying and navigating both text and graphical internal references, achieving 90.8% and 81.7% accuracy, respectively, when tested on documents in English, German, and French.

XLNet extends the success of BERT by addressing its limitations in preserving long-term dependencies and addressing issues in specific task areas. This work introduces BERT with Adaptive Layer Scaling (BALSA), a new architecture that incorporates adaptive scaling factors for each layer, allowing the model to learn more effectively from data. Our results demonstrate that this approach significantly improves performance in tasks requiring long-term memory, such as machine reading comprehension and language modeling, while also reducing the number of parameters required for training compared to BERT. These findings suggest that BARCH can serve as a strong baseline for future research in natural language processing tasks involving long-term dependencies and efficient model design.

The discovery of exoplanets via the radial velocity technique relies on detecting minute stellar wobbles that are easily obscured by stellar activity or contamination from stellar lines in exoplanetary spectra. Undulatory fluid propulsion is a prevalent mechanism in nature, yet the dominant influence exerted either by fluid inertia or fluid waves remains debated. This study examines fluid wave drag on flexible, undulating swimmers via numerical simulations, revealing that the inertia of fluid waves is significantly more potent than inertia alone. This finding elucidates the fluid wave-driven propulsion mode in flapping swimmers and enables a streamlined potential flow model for the drag on swimmers. Applying this framework to simulations, we analyzed the swimming kinematics and performance of various species, including the inchworm, eel, lamprey, shark, and snake. Determining the population of massive galaxies at redshifts exceeding 3 is crucial for understanding the early universe, yet current surveys struggle to detect them due to limitations in detector size and exposure duration. To overcome these barriers, we propose a new survey design that utilizes a large telescope equipped with a high-throughput detector and leverages long-term tracking to fully exploit deep imaging capabilities. By employing a novel algorithm to optimize the placement of transient point sources, we can efficiently populate deep imaging fields. Our simulations indicate that a telescope with a 3-meter primary mirror, operating at wavelengths from 0.6 to 2.5 $\mu$m, could identify over 1,000 galaxies brighter than $m_{AB} = 27$ within an area of 10 square degrees. This enhanced survey capability would significantly improve our understanding of the early cosmic census during the reionization epoch.

We introduce a novel framework for seven-dimensional gravity that accommodates two distinct but equivalent formalisms: a first-order approach utilizing the connection and Riemann curvature, and a second-order method based on the Weyl tensor. By exploring the seven-dimensional anti-de Sitter space within this system, we derive corresponding six-dimensional and five-dimensional solutions. Additionally, our analysis yields valid seven-, six-, and five-dimensional configurations featuring geometries such as flat spaculations, Coulomb-like fields, warping, and specific compactification patterns.

We investigate the jamming dynamics of disks confined within a rectangular box where the objects possess varying masses and the influence is driven by a vertically falling probe. The system reaches a compacted state, limited only by the available space, where the angle each disk makes with the box floor is determined by the disk's mass relative to gravity. The study examines how the probe penetrates the depth of this jammed configuration as a function of the mass distribution. Additionally, the work analyzes the mechanical response of individual disks to vertical compression forces acting on the system.

El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the primary driver of El Niño and La Niña events, which are distinguished by opposing sea surface temperature anomalies in the equatorial Pacific. These phenomena significantly alter global weather patterns, particularly precipitation. This study utilizes a 100-member ensemble generated from an operational coupled climate model to analyze the distinct characteristics of the two phases. The results demonstrate that temperature anomalies in the central Pacific are more critical in shaping precipitation differences than those observed in the eastern Pacific. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the zonal asymmetry of heat release in the tropical Pacific is the fundamental mechanism responsible for the divergent precipitation responses to the two phases. The findings underscore the pivotal role of central Pacific temperature anomalies in defining precipitation variability between El Niño and La Niña events.

The classical understanding of small deformations relies on the principle of objectivity and material frame indifference (MFI), which posits that the internal state of a linearly elastic medium remains unaffected by a spatial frame rotation. However, recent advances in synthetic soft matter have revealed that even elastic processes can exhibit nonaffinity—the deviation of internal degrees of freedom from average macroscopic motion. We present an accessible experimental method to verify the emergence of nonaffinity within the elastic regime. Our findings indicate that when elastic responses violate MFI, the internal energy of a weakly driven, finite-sized soft system becomes contingent upon the orientation of the reference frame. Specifically, we utilized a cryogenic electron microscope to drive a frozen colloidal flock with a frame-dependent elastic distortion and tracked the resulting internal rearrangements via high-resolution imaging. The resulting data confirmed clear nonaffinity within the linear elastic regime, demonstrating a breaking of MFI manifesting as an internal energy that varies with reference frame orientation. This phenomenon, driven by a hysteresis-induced breakdown of symmetric internal stresses, represents a departure from the universal consensus that small deformations are inherently affine. Consequently, violating MFI within the elastic domain introduces new complexities into the theoretical modeling of the universal elastic properties of soft solids.

This paper examines a specific class of stochastic reaction-diffusion systems for single-population species, focusing on establishing conditions that guarantee both global existence and uniqueness of positive solutions as well as their long-term dynamics, or stochastically bounded properties. We demonstrate that, unlike typical models where introducing stochastic elements precludes a weak solution to the corresponding deterministic system, these specific conditions can still be met even when the system is fully deterministic. Additionally, we derive sufficient conditions ensuring that the second moments of the population density remain uniformly bounded over time, provided the model parameters and data exhibit polynomial growth. Finally, we establish the ergodicity of the associated Markov process, provided the system satisfies a weak Feller property.

This paper introduces a new methodology for deriving algebraic semantics within many-valued and many-sorted fuzzy logisms. Utilizing this approach, we first construct the category of many-valued and many-valued free algebras; subsequently, we demonstrate that every algebra belonging to these varieties falls into a computable complexity class. Specifically, we establish that the algebraic complexity of fuzzy logic MTL is P, whereas the algebraic complexity of the standard subfuzzy logic BL$_0$ is EXPSPACE. Additionally, we formulate and establish a universal hypothesis regarding algebraic complexities for subfluz logicals derived from BL$_0$ and BL.
